parts.text: A student investigates the period of a pendulum. Fig. 1.1 and Fig. 1.2 show the arrangement. one complete oscillation clamp clamp floor x bob d l Fig. 1.1 Fig. 1.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: (a) The student measures the distance d between the bottom of the clamp and the floor. 120.0 cm d = .............................................................. This distance d remains constant throughout the experiment. He adjusts the length l of the pendulum to 70.0 cm. Calculate the distance x between the centre of the pendulum bob and the floor. Record the value of x in the first row of Table 1.1. [1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: (b) The student displaces the bob slightly and releases it so that it swings. Fig. 1.2 shows one complete oscillation of the pendulum. He measures, and records in the first row of Table 1.1, the time t for 10 complete oscillations.

parts.label: i
parts.text: (i) Calculate, and record in the first row of Table 1.1, the period T of the pendulum. The period is the time for one complete oscillation. [1]

parts.label: ii
parts.text: (ii) Calculate, and record in the first row of Table 1.1, T 2 . [2]

ms.label: 1(b)(ii)
ms.text:
T = 2.79 (or 2.789 or 2.7889)
2
T given to 3 significant figures

parts.label: c
parts.text: (c) He repeats the procedure using x = 45.0 cm, 40.0 cm, 35.0 cm and 30.0 cm. He records the readings in Table 1.1. Plot a graph of T 2 ( y -axis) against x ( x -axis). You do not need to start your axes at the origin (0,0). [4]

ms.label: 1(c)
ms.text:
Graph:
Axes correctly labelled with quantity and unit and right way round
Suitable scales
All the plots from their table correct to better than ½ small square
Good line judgement, thin, continuous line

ms.label: 1(e)
ms.text: (Timing) errors less significant / have a smaller percentage uncertainty / the error is spread over 10 periods / is divided by 10
